newsitem.title: USA: Brazzaville frontline close to U.S. embassy.
newsitem.headline: Brazzaville frontline close to U.S. embassy.

text.p: The Army general overseeing a U.S. military mission to Brazzaville on Wednesday described a shifting frontline between rebels and government forces, which was about two blocks from the U.S. embassy.

Officials on the ground in Congo said the line of conflict was shifting, according to Brig. Gen. Geoffrey Lambert, who on Tuesday directed an airlift of 56 Americans and other foreigners from the capital, Brazzaville, to Libreville, Gabon.

Lambert said the officials put the current line of conflict about "a block and a half, two blocks" from the U.S. embassy, where the State Department said 15 diplomats remained. "It's a moving confrontation line right now," Lambert said.
He said there was "considerable firing ... lots of fighting on the street" at 9 a.m. EDT (1300 GMT) on Wednesday.

Lambert, based in Stuttgart, Germany, said the 12-man U.S. military team that flew into Brazzaville on Tuesday had to circle the airport for 10 minutes while French officials on the ground monitored gunfire aimed at the airport's fire station.

Speaking to reporters at the Pentagon by telephone, Lambert said no gunfire was aimed directly at the C-130 cargo plane, even though planes had landed at the Brazzaville airfield as recently as Monday "full of holes."
The fighting in Brazzaville has pitted soldiers loyal to President Pascal Lissouba and allied militias against the militia of former president Denis Sassou Nguesso.

In a clear sign that Washington believed Sassou Nguesso was in the wrong, the State Department on Wednesday said it deeply regretted that "rebel groups, opposition groups, have decided to take their fight to the streets."

Spokesman Nicholas Burns urged Sassou Nguesso to accept a ceasefire announced by Lissouba and agree to international mediation. The ex-president later called on his supporters to observe a truce after seven days of fighting.

Lambert said the U.S. military team unloaded supplies, including extra rations and communications equipment, and evacuated 56 people: 30 Americans, 10 Zaireans, five Italians, four French, two Gabonese, and one each from the Central African Republic, the Netherlands, Senegal, Zambia and the United Kingdom. They also airlifted one dog, Lambert said.
The plane was on the ground for 26 minutes, then flew to Libreville, where six other U.S. forces were stationed as part of a total team of 18, Lambert said.
He said the team was "awaiting instructions" while on the ground in Libreville.
The clashes began on June 5 after soldiers surrounded Sassou Nguesso's home as part of a crackdown on militias and illegal arms ahead of a July 27 presidential election.
